title: Mitigation measures for bromate formation during wastewater ozonation and impact on micropollutant elimination
content: Negative impacts of micropollutants on aquatic ecosystems and the role of wastewater treatment plants as point sources are well documented. Ozonation has proven highly effective in eliminating micropollutants during wastewater treatment. However, concerns about the formation of transformation products such as bromate, a potentially carcinogenic oxidation by-product, are increasing, particularly problematic in catchment areas with elevated bromide concentrations. Developing effective mitigation techniques to reduce bromate formation remains a key challenge for the safe application of ozonation. This study investigates mitigation strategies based on monochloramine (NH2Cl), ammonia (NH3), and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), applied with single and serial ozone dosing at laboratory scale and in a pilot-plant equipped with the Ozone Strong Water (OSW) system. Serial ozone dosing consistently reduced bromate formation compared with single dosing, with reductions exceeding 50% under some conditions. Among the tested chemical strategies, NH3 achieved the highest bromate reduction of up to 66% in laboratory experiments, followed by H2O2 and NH2Cl with reductions of approximately 50%. These trends were largely confirmed at pilot scale. Micropollutant elimination was not significantly affected by the mitigation strategies at pilot scale, although NH3 addition reduced the mean elimination by up to 30% in laboratory experiments. The results demonstrate the potential of combining serial ozone dosing with targeted chemical mitigation to reduce bromate formation, particularly in bromide-rich conditions, while adhering to bromate regulatory limits.
